# 1 Chronicles Chapter 19 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 380v

---

**1** Some time later, King Nahash of Ammon died, and his son succeeded him.

**2** David thought, "I should show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, since his father was kind to me." So David sent a delegation to express sympathy over his father's death. But when David's men arrived in Ammonite territory to convey condolences to Hanun,

**3** the Ammonite commanders said to Hanun, "Do you really believe David is honoring your father by sending these men to comfort you? They're spies! He sent them to scout out the land so he can invade and destroy it."

**4** So Hanun seized David's envoys, shaved off their beards, and cut off their garments at the waist, exposing them. Then he sent them away in disgrace.

**5** When David learned what had happened, he sent word to meet the men — they were too humiliated to return home. The king told them, "Stay in Jericho until your beards grow back. Then come home."

**6** The Ammonites realized they had made themselves an enemy of David. So Hanun and the Ammonites sent a thousand talents of silver to hire chariots and cavalry from Mesopotamia, Aram-maacah, and Zobah.

**7** They hired thirty-two thousand chariots, along with the king of Maacah and his forces. This army arrived and set up camp near Medeba. The Ammonites also mustered their own troops from their towns and marched out to fight.

**8** When David heard about this, he sent Joab with the entire elite army.

**9** The Ammonites deployed for battle at the city gate, while the hired kings positioned themselves separately in the open country.

**10** Joab saw that he faced enemies both ahead and behind him. So he selected Israel's finest warriors and lined them up against the Arameans.

**11** He placed the rest of the forces under his brother Abishai's command, deploying them against the Ammonites.

**12** Joab said to his brother, "If the Arameans overpower me, come rescue me. If the Ammonites overpower you, I'll come rescue you.

**13** Be brave! Let's fight with everything we have — for our people and for the cities of our God. And may the LORD do what he sees as right."

**14** Joab advanced against the Arameans, and they broke and ran before him.

**15** When the Ammonites saw the Arameans running, they fled from Abishai as well and retreated into the city. Joab then returned to Jerusalem.

**16** The Arameans, realizing they had been routed by Israel, sent for reinforcements from beyond the Euphrates River. Shophach, the commander of Hadadezer's army, led them.

**17** When David received this report, he assembled all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and advanced against them. He drew up his forces facing the Arameans, and they engaged him in battle.

**18** But the Arameans fled before Israel. David's forces killed seven thousand charioteers and forty thousand infantry. David also killed Shophach, the army commander.

**19** When Hadadezer's vassal kings saw that Israel had defeated them, they surrendered to David and became his subjects. After that, the Arameans refused to help the Ammonites ever again.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 2-4 — Diplomacy destroyed:** David's gesture of *chesed* (loyal kindness) is met with suspicion and public humiliation. The shaving of beards and cutting of garments is not merely rude — it is a calculated act of political warfare. In the ancient Near East, a man's beard was his honor; to shave it was to unmake him socially. The exposure of the lower body was an added degradation. David's ambassadors are symbolically stripped of their manhood and dignity.

**Verse 12-13 — Joab at his best:** This is Joab's finest moment in Scripture. Caught between two armies, he divides his forces, commits to mutual rescue, and then surrenders the outcome to God. "May the LORD do what he sees as right" — this is battlefield theology at its purest. No presumption, no guarantee of victory — just courage and trust.

**Verse 19 — The war ends with a word:** "They made peace with David and became subject to him." What began with a failed act of kindness ends with enforced submission. The Chronicler draws no moral — the reader is left to ponder the distance between *chesed* offered and conquest achieved.

*— PNEUMA*
